target_customer: Women who want prescription birth control and later other women's health treatments prescribed online and delivered, paying through insurance or cash
problem: Getting birth control meant a clinic visit and a pharmacy trip, which is hard in places with few providers. Nurx let patients answer medical questions online, had a clinician prescribe and shipped the medication to the door.
business_model: Telemedicine consultation and prescription fulfillment, paid by insurance or by patients, with sales of medication and testing kits

founders.name: Edvard Engesaeth
founders.background_notes: Listed as the only founder on the YC page; a physician per one profile.

founders.name: Hans Gangeskar
founders.background_notes: Named as co-founder in two secondary profiles; not on the YC page.

competitors.name: Maven
competitors.what: Women's health app with online clinician access

competitors.name: PillPack
competitors.what: Pharmacy that packages and delivers medications

competitors.name: Planned Parenthood app
competitors.what: Birth control ordering and refill app

technical_complexity.rationale: A consumer app with clinician workflow, state by state licensing and pharmacy fulfillment, which is mostly operational and regulatory complexity rather than hard technology.

defensibility.rationale: Licensing, pharmacy and insurance billing take time to build, but rivals could copy the model, and many did.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Many telehealth rivals appeared later, and in February 2022 Nurx merged all-stock into Thirty Madison instead of being copied away by a single incumbent.

market_need_then: Access to birth control was limited by clinic visits and in some states by few providers, and phones and apps were becoming a normal way to order services.

branding.domain_note: Uses nurx.com; acquisition history not found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Warm, reassuring and non-judgmental, stressing patient-first care

branding.brand_signature: Early Uber for birth control framing in press
branding.community_and_virality: Large press coverage of the app, over 2 million patients and tens of thousands of five-star reviews claimed on its own site; no merch or fan community found.

brand_strength.rationale: Well known in telehealth for women's health with a registered trademark and large review count, but the invented name has spelling and pronunciation friction and the company now sits under Thirty Madison.

pivots.to: Broader women's health services such as menopause, skincare and weight management
pivots.why: Expansion of services beyond the first product; reasons inferred from the product pages, not stated.

outcome_analysis: Nurx started as birth control delivery in late 2015, raised a 5.3 million dollar Series A from Union Square in 2016, 36 million in 2018 and a 52 million round in 2019 at a valuation near 300 million. In February 2022 it merged all-stock into Thirty Madison, under which it remains a brand, while rivals like The Pill Club later failed. The terms were not disclosed, so whether the merger was a strong exit is unknown.
notes: The 52 million round of August 2019 is called Series B in one press release and Series C by Becker's and Fenwick; recorded as series_c. Pre-merger valuation of 322.5 or 332 million appears in single sources and is unverified. Founder list conflicts: YC page names only Engesaeth, secondary profiles add Hans Gangeskar and another lists Susan Coelius Keplinger. The 2018 pivot entry is not directly sourced as a pivot. Competitor list comes from one 2016 Ohio report; Hers, The Pill Club and Lemonaid were not found in dated sources. One site claims Thirty Madison shut the Nurx brand down, contradicted by the live Nurx site showing Nurx as a Thirty Madison company with 2026 copyright.
